content: This is a discssuion thread for #Project announcements > Nerodia: Lean to Python (Preview)

Hey @Mac Malone ! Very cool project! I’d be happy to test it. What is the intended long-term scope: module-level functions only, or also Python classes, stateful Lean objects, callbacks, and zero-copy array interoperability? How much of the current API is stable enough for downstream experimentation, and which platforms or workflows would be most useful to test right now?

Thank you for your interest! :heart:

How much of the current API is stable enough for downstream experimentation

The current API is meant to be reasonably stable, but limited. Renames and removals will go through a deprecation period, and other breaking changes only made when necessary. There is even a test fixture which tracks changes to the public API. Important caveats are that anything in the namespaces Nerodia.Internal and Nerodia.Compiler is unstable and the bodies of definitions which are exposed bu irreducible (ii.e., @[irreducible, expose] ) are not part of the public API. Definitions may also move between related modules without significant warning. All of this will be more firmly documented in a reference manual that will come within the next month.

What is the intended long-term scope: module-level functions only, or also Python classes, stateful Lean objects, callbacks, and zero-copy array interoperability?

Crreating Python classes (and types more generally) will be supported in the future. There will at least be APIs for doing so. I am yet unsure on what DSL elements will be supported. Feel free to suggest what you would like to see! In general, I plan to extend the API to cover most of what PyO3 has in terms of types and methods. A wrapper for Lean objects is also planned.

I am not exactly sure what you mean by "zero-copy array interoperability". The eventual PyTuple will have pure zero-copy element accesses and there will be monadic getItem/setItem for Python objects (e.g., PyList). Nonetheless, Array and Python objects will never be strictly interchangable without copying because Array has a fixed runtime representation distinct from Python objects (and I see no way to resolve that).

I am also happy to factor requests into how I prioritize API elements to implement. If there exsits a particular blocker for a project you would like to test, please feel free to file an issue (or have an AI do so), and I will try to accomdate.

which platforms or workflows would be most useful to test right now?

Ideally, what I'd like to see is people building, packing, and publishing source distributions and wheels across the platforms Lean supports and reporting on what worked, what did not, and what documentation they would like to see (for eventual inclusion in the reference manual).
Does this ultimately work via python c extension modules, code-generation of python source code, or by generated wrappers that speak to a lean subprocess?
C extension modules (a la PyO3 / setuptools-rust).
In that case, does this move Lean module finalizers any closer to an RFC (since python modules can be finalized and reinitialized)

No, that has not been dicussed. The current approach is just to try to ensure idempotency on reinit. Teardown of modules and Lean was so big of change I never even considered proposing it. (Though perhaps I should?)
Oh, this is a super cool project! I'm curious! have you seen https://github.com/BasisResearch/lean.py?

@Kiran Yes, I have! From what I observed, Nerodia and lean.py target different use cases. lean.py seems designed to faciliate scripted interaction between Lean and Python. Nerodia, on the other hand, builds compiled wheels, so Python users can install Lean packages without a Lean toolchain (or even necessarily knowing the library they are using is Lean-based).
Gotcha gotcha! Yes, that was my reading too! Was just curious if you were aware! This is super cool, looking forward to seeing what Lean projects end up permeating into the Python ecosystem!
@Mac Malone Thanks for the detailed answer! :) I’ll definitely check it out and try building and packaging it on a few platforms. I’ll report any issues or documentation feedback I run into!
does the lib support invocation of python callbacks or pure functions?
@Mac Malone Does this allow the Lean code to call Python functions. Concretely, can I write stubs of these in Lean (say using opaque) so that the generated Python code will call them?

@Siddhartha Gadgil What do you mean by "these" in "stubs of these"? Regardless, Nerodia does provide (a currently limited set of) bindings to the Python C API. This how it exposes Lean calls to Python. So, yes, Lean code can (and does) call Python functions.

By "these" I mean Python functions. Suppose I have a function in Python computing minimal prime factor say, it would be nice if in Lean I could say opaque min_prime_factor: Nat -> Nat so that in the generated Python code the correct Python function gets called.
This will mean that opaque commands are dropped.

The general sketch of how this would usually work with the Python C API is something like the following:

primelib.py

def min_prime_factor(n: int) -> int:
  ...

PrimeFactor.lean

import Nerodia

open Nerodia

def minPrimeFactor (n : Nat) : IO Nat := PyIO.toIO do
  let primelib <- Nerodia.import "primelib"
  let fn <- primelib..getAttrByString "min_prime_factor"
  let factor : PyObject <- fn.call1 (<- mkPyNat n)
  return (<- factor.int).toInt.toNat

As a caveat, calling arbitrary Python functions is not yet part of the Nerodia's current small API (i.e., call1 does not exist yet), but it will soonish. Is this close enough to what you are looking for? Unlike Lean's @[extern] functions for C, Python functions (defined in Python) cannot be linked to indvidually (CPython does not support this). The module they are contained in needs to be loaded first. This could be wrapped into some macro to be made prettier, but there is a cost here worth keeping track of.
@Mac Malone This is useful, but ideally I want to avoid going to IO level. I realize that is impossible in Lean at a conceptual level, but for running code it would be useful.
My naive thinking was that if something is opaque in Lean but implemented in Python, when calling from Python we could redirect to the Python implementation.

You could also do something like this:

import Nerodia

open Nerodia

intiialize primelib : PyObject <- PyIO.toIO do
  Nerodia.import "primelib"

initialize minPrimeFactor._fn : PyObject <- PyIO.toIO do
  primelib..getAttrByString "min_prime_factor"

def minPrimeFactor._io (n : Nat) : IO Nat := PyIO.toIO do
  return (<- (<- _fn.call1 (<- mkPyNat n)).int).toInt.toNat

def minPrimeFactor (n : Nat) : Nat :=
  match unsafe unsafeIO (_io n) with
  | .ok n => n
  | .error e => panic! (toString e)
@Mac Malone Thanks a lot. This works perfectly I believe. I did not know about unsafeIO. I will look it up.
